messages.subject: Feature request: Neal's overrelaxation for conjugate samplers
messages.subject_clean: Feature request: Neal's overrelaxation for conjugate samplers
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nimble devs,

Neal describes a way to reduce the random walk of a Gibbs sampler by using overrelaxation, which seems very effective:

https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~radford/overk.abstract.html
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-5014-9_8

His strategy, §5, seems especially suitable for samplers based on conjugacy, or for which the cumulative distribution function is available, as some of those used by Nimble. From what I've seen it seems that Nimble doesn't implement it at the moment. It seems that it would make Nimble even faster, so I'd like to propose it for future Nimble development.

I will try to create a Nimble sampler that implements it, and report on performance results – although this will take probably some time.

Cheers and happy new year to you all,
Luca

Yes, unless you get into using the nimbleExternalCall function, to call arbitrary C++ code from your density function, then I think you'll be restricted to the standard numerical operations which are supported by the NIMBLE DSL.   That said, doing as much of the pre-computation *once* in advance will definitely be helpful.

So, it's true that the finite interval of support defined in (1) is constant?  And therefore, the set of integers within this range are also unchanging?

I'm guessing, then, the reason (2) must be repeated on each call to the distribution is because the mean and variance defining the normal distribution are changing?  In that case, I'm not thinking of any obvious way around evaluating the normal density at each integer, and returning the correct normalized value.

> Daniel,
>
> Thanks for the insight; I think it suggests something to try. My distribution is a discretized version of a normal distribution. The implementation of the d function is essentially this:
>
> 1) Define a finite range of support for the distribution.
> 2) Create a vector of normal densities for all integers within the range.
> 3) Standardize the vector created in (2) by dividing each element by the sum of its elements.
> 4) Look up the vector element corresponding to a particular integer and return it.
>
> (2) Has to be done each time the density function is called, and if the distribution has a large range of support, then that's a lot of calls to repeat. An obvious solution in C++ is to create something like a std::map where key={integer in range}, value={corresponding element from standardized vector in (3)} and store that map for future use. I'm not sure how to do that with Nimble, though.

messages.subject: Re: Deterministic nodes with NA values
messages.body_plain:
Hannah, thanks for your email.  It's impossible to say exactly what's happening, without being able to run a reproducible example.  But from everything you said, it seems to me that something on the right-hand-side of the declaration of log(f_ne[i,j]) must itself be NA.  This could include any *one* of beta.n[1], beta.n[2], etc... for for example if you initial value vector for the vector beta.n is only length 5, for example, then it's believable that beta.n[6] would be NA, thus causing all the downstream NA's you're seeing.  Otherise, if not a beta.n[i] term, then I think it would have to be one of the (matrix) covariates, such as weekend2[], or otherwise.  If you simply forgot to provide an initial value for one of these covariates (weekend2, or otherwise), then it would cause everything you're seeing.  That could also be a likely culprit, if you just updated the covariates (from vectors to matrices), and perhaps forgot to provide one, or simply spelled the name wrong.

I hope this helps.  If you can provide a reproducible example, then I'm sure we can nail down the problem.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
hi Luca,

One of our main challenges in adding new samplers is less our developer time in coding the samplers and more knowing which samplers are worth investing in, and (in the common case that a sampler has tuning parameters) choosing good default values for those.

So, yes, we'd be very happy to hear what you find in terms of performance of the overrelaxation strategy. In particular, it will be important to know if any improvement in mixing overcomes any additional computation time for doing the overrelaxation.

And a final note that in many problems, the issue is dependence between parameters; it sounds like this approach is focused on one-at-a-time univariate sampling.

-chris

Hey Cecilia,

Your guess about your problem was correct, the primary issue was that your initial latent state assignments (zinits) were suggesting that certain transitions were possible (e.g., from 1 ->3) but the model defined them as impossible causing the those pesky -infinite values to pop up.

Here is my suggestion that will at least let you get in the gears moving. I don't believe I changed anything else except for the following lines of code.

# Fill in the known states
zinits <- y

# For all missed observations, assign the latent state to be the latent state during the time period prior, which overwrites itself.
for(i in 1:nrow(y)){
  for(j in (first[i]+1):ncol(y)){
    if(y[i,j] == 0){
      zinits[i,j] <- zinits[i,j-1]
    }
  }
}

# Lastly, given that these appear to be daily observations, you may want to limit the initial values for the other parameters to be on the high end. You may run into issues in model runs if the initial draw for survival is really low. Here I just set them to be constant values, but you don't have to do this.
initial.values <- function(){list(phiJ = 0.9,
                                  phiP = 0.9,
                                  phiA = 0.9,
                                  psiJP = .5,
                                  psiPA = .5,
                                  pJ = .95,
                                  pP = .95,
                                  pA = .95,
                                  z = zinits)}

Hope this helps,

-Dan

Hi Chris,

Thank you!  Please see below for reproducable code.... it first simulates some 'death' times from the expoential distribution, then formats it ready for the model and then fits in NIMBLE... the WAIC I get matches exactly other models that I fit (for example with the custom distribution that I used above) and the pWAIC is always 0?

R code for WAIC comparisons:

library(tidyverse)
library(nimble)

## set up right censored data Exponential distributed data
## set parameters
r <- 0.005
censorRate <- 0.1
nind <- 500

## create sims
sims <- rexp(nind, r = r)

## censor results (1 = interval, 2 = right)
censored <- rbinom(length(sims), 1, censorRate) + 1

## adjust death times to make interval censored
sims <- ceiling(sims)

## adjust sims with random right-censored time
adjust <- which(censored == 2)
sims[adjust] <- sapply(sims[adjust], function(x) {
  sample(1:x, 1)
})

## setup data
tD <- rep(NA, length(sims))
tL <- sims - 1
tU <- sims

## define censoring matrices
## (here tL is lower bound and tU upper bound
## and sims is censoring time for right-censored
## so no further adjustments needed)
cint <- cbind(tL, tU)
colnames(cint) <- NULL
cint[censored == 2, 1] <- 0

## set up zL/zU input matrix
zL <- tL
zL[censored == 2] <- tU[censored == 2]

zU <- tU
zU[censored == 2] <- NA

## set maximum observation time
tM <- rep(ceiling(max(sims) + 1), length(sims))

##########################################################
##                                                      ##
## Now fit exponential model back to the data in NIMBLE ##
##                                                      ##
##########################################################

code <- nimbleCode({
  ## survival components for dead badgers

  for (i in 1:nind) {

    ## likelihood for interval-truncated exponential

    censored[i] ~ dinterval(tD[i], cint[i, ])

    tD[i] ~ dexp(r)
  }

  ## priors
  r ~ dexp(1)
})

## set up other components of model
consts <- list(nind = nind)
data <- list(cint = cint, censored = censored, tD = tD)

## find overdispersed initial values
tinitFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  apply(cbind(cint, censored), 1, function(x) {
    if(x[3] == 2) {
      y <- x[2] + 1
    } else {
      y <- runif(1, x[1], x[2])
    }
    y
  })
}
initFn <- function(cint, censored) {
  ## get ML estimates as initial values
  optFn <- function(pars, t) {
    if(any(pars < 0)) {
      return(NA)
    }
    sum(dexp(t, r = pars[1], log = TRUE))
  }
  pars <- list(convergence = 1)
  k <- 0
  while(pars$convergence != 0 & k < 20) {
    ## sample missing values
    tD <- tinitFn(cint, censored)
    pars <- optim(rexp(1, 100), optFn, t = tD, control = list(fnscale = -1))
    k <- k + 1
  }
  if(k == 20) {
    stop("Can't sample initial values")
  }
  pars <- pars$par
  list(
    tD = tD,
    r = pars[1]
  )
}

## define the model, data, inits and constants
model <- nimbleModel(code = code, constants = consts, data = data, inits = initFn(cint, censored))

## compile the model

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

I don't believe WAIC makes sense here. You don't have any data (i.e., all of your tD values are missing). So the only contribution to the likelihood in the model is from "data$censored", but each of these always gives a likelihood contribution of 1 (a log-likelihood contribution of 0) because (based on the model construction, using dinterval) only values of tD that satisfy the censoring constraints are sampled. WAIC is calculated based on the density of the observations given the values of the sampled parameters at each iteration. In this case that is the density of the "censored" elements given the sampled "tD" elements.

If you want to use WAIC here, I think you need at least some of the tD values to be observed to be specific values.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Great questions, Emanuele.  While many properties of the NIMBLE samplers, including the univariate RWMH sampler, are easily configurable using the "control list", the target acceptance rate is not among them.  The easiest (and quite straightforward) way to change this would be:
- Copy the source code for the sampler_RW function <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/ca9b4067ceaca97040782e686aadfe5b6648926e/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L190> to your R script
- Rename this sampler to something else (perhaps sampler_RW2, or otherwise)
- Change the optimalAR variable in the setup function, to whatever alternate target acceptance rate you desire
- Modify your MCMC configuration object, to use this sampler, sampler_RW2, instead of the default RW sampler, using functions such as conf$removeSampler(...), and conf$addSampler(...)

Alternatively, you could quite easily make the optimalAR be configurable, by adding a line at the beginning of the setup function:
optimalAR <- extractControlElement(control, 'optimalAR', 0.44)    ## 0.44 is the default

Then removing the later line in the step function:
optimalAR <- 0.44

Then, you can specify whatever target acceptance rate you desire, at the time of adding the sampler:
conf$addSampler(target = NODE_TO_SAMPLE, type = "RW2", optimalAR = 0.5)

Truth be told, this is a change we perhaps could / should make to NIMBLE's codebase, just to make this target acceptance rate easily modifiable.  That's something I could do, although I'd want to discuss it with the rest of the development team first.

As for different acceptance rates for higher dimensional MH sampling, take a look at the code for the RW_block sampler <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/ca9b4067ceaca97040782e686aadfe5b6648926e/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L349>, which dynamically sets the target acceptance rate, based upon the dimension of the MH update.  I think that will answer your question, but I'm happy to discuss further, if that's helpful.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

Perhaps what you want is a model that gives the probability of observing a given observation, which in your case is the probability of observing that the value is in an interval since you don't know the value exactly. That probability would be the integral over the known censoring interval of some distribution that represents the potential value of the observation, which you could hopefully compute in closed form. I.e., that distribution would be the distribution you would use for the likelihood in the situation where you imagine you could actually know the exact value of the observation (in your model code you are using an exponential). So if you could code up models specified in that way, I think you could use WAIC to compare such models.

-chris

> - Copy the source code for the sampler_RW function <https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/ca9b4067ceaca97040782e686aadfe5b6648926e/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_samplers.R#L190> to your R script

> - Change the optimalAR variable in the setup function, to whatever alternate target acceptance rate you desire
> - Modify your MCMC configuration object, to use this sampler, sampler_RW2, instead of the default RW sampler, using functions such as conf$removeSampler(...), and conf$addSampler(...)
>
> Alternatively, you could quite easily make the optimalAR be configurable, by adding a line at the beginning of the setup function:
> optimalAR <- extractControlElement(control, 'optimalAR', 0.44)    ## 0.44 is the default

> optimalAR <- 0.44
>
> Then, you can specify whatever target acceptance rate you desire, at the time of adding the sampler:
> conf$addSampler(target = NODE_TO_SAMPLE, type = "RW2", optimalAR = 0.5)

Hi,

A bit late to add this, but I just wanted to add that I don't think this is correct for setting the seed in parallel processing using the parallel package:

1) In the `parLapply` call, the values of `X` are the values used for
the `seed` function. So it is used.

I've tried this and it produces different results across MCMC simulations.

What I've found that works for repeatable results using parallel processing is to add this just after making the cluster:

e.g.,

this_cluster <- makeCluster(2)

clusterSetRNGStream(cl = this_cluster, 500) # note that 500 could be any integer.

So, I don't think the X in parLapply actually does anything to produce repeatable results, whereas using this builtin function of the parallel package provides reproducible results.

Cheers,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
You're exactly right, Keith - those options are not available when using nimbleMCMC.  The nimbleMCMC interface is designed only for running the "default" MCMC, which involves no customization of the MCMC sampling algorithms themselves.  If you want to delve deeper into customizing the MCMC sampling strategies, then you're right, the workflow to use is:

nimbleModel
configureMCMC
buildMCMC
compileNimble
runMCMC

I know this is more steps than a single call to nimbleMCMC, but the changes from using nimbleMCMC to the functional workflow above are quite mechanical.  If more direction on how/where the various arguments to those functions should be organized, then just let me know - no problem at all.

Cheers,
Daniel

hi Dan,

Thanks for commenting here.

I've checked the example and I do get reproducible results using the code provided. I'm wondering if you modified it such that you are creating random initial values? If so, you'd need to use set.seed before you generate the initial values within the run_MCMC_allcode function.

One other note is that the approach in that example relies on simply setting different seeds for the different chains. While this is probably safe, it is possible that the random numbers generated for one chain could partially overlap the random numbers generated for another chain. Even if this happened, I don't think it would cause substantive dependence between the chains. But your approach of using clusterSetRNGStream has the nice feature of ensuring the sequences of random numbers for each of the worker processes won't overlap.

-chris

Rémi, thanks for the question.  It looks like seq() doesn't go through compilation, so try changing your nlchoose function to use the ":" operator, instead:

I also added the "returnType(double(0))" statement, which you should have as well, to specify the scalar return type of the function.

nlchoose <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(n = double(0), k = double(0)){
        returnType(double(0))
        # if(any(is.na <http://is.na>(c(n,k)))) return(NA)
        if(k != 0) {
            n <- round(n)
            k <- round(k)
            return(sum(log((n-k+1):n)) - sum(log(1:k)))
        } else {
            return(0)
        }
    }
)

I think this should work for you, but let us know if you still have problems.

Cheers,
Daniel
